blocks.text: Exhaustion is not completion

Two independent tests can stop a recursive call. The completion test asks whether the current path already satisfies the result contract. Candidate exhaustion asks whether this incomplete path has any legal child. Here completion is false and no child exists, so the branch is a dead end and contributes no result.

Returning from the call transfers control to its parent. The parent restores any state changed for this branch and continues with the next sibling candidate. Nothing about this local failure invalidates choices elsewhere in the search tree.

A valid result must pass the completion contract, which the prompt explicitly says this state does not. Restarting from the root would repeat work and discard the parent’s remaining siblings. blocks.text: Separate tree width from path depth

At the root, any of n values may fill the first position. After one choice, n - 1 values remain; then n - 2, down to one final choice. The number of complete leaves is therefore n × (n - 1) × ... × 1 = n!, so the leaves dimension is O(n!).

Along any one root-to-leaf path, exactly one position is filled per recursive level. A complete permutation contains n choices, so at most a linear number of calls are simultaneously active. Whether one counts n choice levels or n + 1 call frames including the root, the maximum recursion depth is O(n).

These answers do not claim the entire algorithm runs in only O(n!) time. If each emitted permutation is copied into an output collection, copying n values per leaf contributes O(n · n!) output work. The prompt asks only for leaf count and live recursion depth.

O(2^n) describes binary include/exclude leaves, not a branch factor that shrinks from n to 1. O(n^n) would allow every value at every position instead of removing used values. The factorial number of leaves does not make one path factorially deep.

Duplicate control answers whether two different legal index branches encode the same value-level output. A unique-permutation solver uses both: used[i] enforces one use per index, while the sorted equal-sibling rule selects a canonical representative among interchangeable occurrences.
They address different semantic problems. Visited state usually enforces branch legality. It commonly appears in combinations and permutations.

The implementation deliberately visits all n! indexed leaves. At each leaf it copies n values and hashes or compares a length-n key, so generation-and-copy work is O(n · n!).

Most appends write into existing capacity in O(1), but an append that triggers geometric growth allocates a larger buffer and copies Θ(n) existing elements. blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Strategy A visits at most n values, so it is O(n). Strategy B costs `O(n)` to copy, `O(n log n)` to comparison-sort, and `O(log n)` to search. Summing gives `O(n + n log n + log n) = O(n log n)`.
Contrast the strategies

O(log n) describes only the final lookup after order exists. For one query, the sorting term dominates, so the correct direct scan has the better complete asymptotic time. O(n²) overstates comparison sorting, while O(n) for Strategy B incorrectly drops its sorting work.
Preprocessing must be amortized across enough reuse before its per-query benefit can matter.

questions.prompt: A sorted array query asks for every value that is prime. Which strategy follows without a separate prime index?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

At midpoint `m`, ascending order turns one comparison into a proof: if `target < a[m]`, every index right of `m` is at least `a[m]` and cannot equal the target; if `target > a[m]`, every index left of `m` is at most `a[m]`. Equality completes the “any match” contract.
Contrast the strategies

Random access makes each midpoint inspection O(1), so repeated legal halving gives O(log n). This proof applies to exact comparison by the sort key, not to every query or helper predicate. It also returns a key-equal occurrence, not necessarily the earliest record from an original ordering that the sorted array did not preserve.
A midpoint comparison is useful only when order turns it into a proof about all elements on one side.

questions.prompt: A sorted array query asks for any exact target and the array supports random access. What additional condition is already satisfied by the standard comparison?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Binary search can find the first and last positions whose key equals the target. Inside that equal-key range, however, key order gives no timestamp order: timestamps `[9,2,7]` are compatible with all three records having the same key.
Contrast the strategies

After finding the range in O(log n), scan its k records in O(k), or maintain each key group ordered by timestamp or annotated with its minimum. Returning any match or the leftmost equal key assumes a secondary ordering that was never stated; sorting by key alone cannot select the timestamp optimum.

The sum is `a[0] + a[1] + ... + a[n-1]`; every term contributes regardless of whether it lies below or above a midpoint. Without a maintained aggregate, omitting an unchecked half can change the answer, so one pass and O(n) additions are required.
Contrast the strategies

Binary search answers a location or boundary query by proving that one side is irrelevant; no side is irrelevant to an uncomputed sum. A stored total or prefix-sum structure can answer prepared aggregate queries efficiently, but that is metadata, not a consequence of sorting.

Contrast the strategies

Returning a boolean or being named `isValid` specifies syntax, not monotonic behavior, and the array’s value order cannot constrain a callback that ignores or opposes that order. questions.prompt: A sorted array query asks for the first element satisfying an arbitrary callback supplied at runtime. Which contract is needed before using binary search?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For every i > 0 before the answer, sortedness and the absence of an earlier change imply `a[i] == a[0]`. At and after the answer, every value is greater than `a[0]`. Therefore `P(i) = (a[i] != a[0])` is false on the initial run and true on the remaining suffix.
Contrast the strategies

Run first-true binary search on indices 1 through n-1 using `a[i] != a[0]`; if no true index exists, report no result. The local predicate `a[i] != a[i-1]` itself is not monotonic because it is true only at each run boundary, so it is the wrong predicate to binary-search. Returning 1 ignores an equal first pair and n < 2, while claiming a scan is the only solution misses the monotonic initial-run boundary.

An aligned predicate proves which half is impossible; efficient random access turns repeated halving into O(log n); output metadata prevents a key-equal but contract-wrong result. blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

At successive levels, finding the midpoint traverses sublists of at most n, n/2, n/4, and so on. Their total is bounded by `n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n`, so all midpoint traversals together are O(n), not O(log n) and not O(n log n).
Contrast the strategies

One ordinary linked-list scan visits at most n nodes, also O(n), and can stop after passing the target. O(n²) overcounts the shrinking sublists as if all levels scanned n nodes; O(n log n) makes the same mistake less severely. Binary-style halving reduces comparisons, but without direct midpoint access it does not improve this worst-case asymptotic time over the scan.
Sum the access work across all levels instead of counting only the number of logical halvings.

In A, an exact match may appear at any position, so inspecting a midpoint gives no basis for discarding either half; one scan costs O(n) and avoids setup. Contrast the strategies

The change is justified by both legality and workload: the representation supplies a half-discard rule, and many queries reuse it. Sorting before every query would instead cost O(n log n) each time; keeping the existing maintained order is what makes the transfer economical.

The key-only binary search is still able to prove that a key exists, but it cannot prove the newly required provenance. This is an output-contract failure, not a midpoint bug. Enriching the representation can make logarithmic lookup legal again.

More comparisons can still cost less when C is usually small relative to H; conversely long shared prefixes can make comparisons expensive. blocks.text: Derive updates and retained entries separately

The scan processes all n occurrences. Each performs one expected O(1) lookup/update, so aggregation costs n · O(1) = O(n) expected time. Emitting k results adds O(k), and k ≤ n, so O(n + k) simplifies to O(n).

Repeated occurrences update an existing counter; only the k distinct keys create entries. The working table therefore uses O(k) auxiliary space even though separate required output storage is excluded. O(1) ignores growing key state, while O(nk) incorrectly multiplies values by groups. Reusable rule: time follows processed occurrences; aggregate space follows distinct retained states.

feedback.reason: Each occurrence performs one expected constant-time update.

blocks.text: Sorting dominates time; its stack dominates workspace
The stated in-place sort costs O(n log n). Afterward, the run scan advances across each of the n positions once, so it adds O(n). Total time is O(n log n + n) = O(n log n).

Mutation permission lets the ordered values remain in the original array, which is not auxiliary storage. The sort's O(log n) stack is live during sorting and the run scan uses only O(1) local state, giving O(log n) peak auxiliary space. O(1) forgets the stated stack; O(n) would add a copy the contract does not require. Reusable rule: simplify time sums and take the largest simultaneously live workspace.

blocks.text: Maintain a set containing exactly the identifiers from earlier arrivals. For each new identifier x, first test whether x is in the set, emit that Boolean for the current stream position, and then insert x. Checking before insertion distinguishes a prior occurrence from the current item, and processing in arrival order preserves the required output order. With a conventional hash set this uses expected O(1) time per arrival and O(k) memory for k distinct identifiers. Sorting can detect duplicates only after accumulating and reordering data, so it misses the immediate per-arrival contract. A hard memory cap or deterministic worst-case requirement would reopen the comparison.

blocks.text: Sorting turns equal values into contiguous runs and orders those runs by value. The reusable rule is to favor ordering when both adjacency and deterministic order are consumed directly by the result.

Memory or worst-case guarantees may affect the final implementation, but the semantic signal is equality-keyed state. Memory-address order is incidental runtime state and cannot replace the missing domain contract.

blocks.text: Sort the values as b[0] ≤ … ≤ b[n−1], then compare each adjacent difference b[i+1] − b[i]. For any nonadjacent pair b[i], b[j] with i < j, the interval between them is a sum of adjacent nonnegative gaps, so at least one adjacent gap is no larger than b[j] − b[i]. Therefore some closest pair is adjacent after sorting. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan O(n); duplicates correctly produce difference zero. A hash table exposes equality, including the zero-distance case, but cannot locate predecessor or successor values needed when the minimum difference is nonzero.

blocks.text: Scan the original sequence from left to right. Maintaining both may improve a large query workload at the price of two representations and synchronized updates. The choice therefore depends on q, k, mutation, memory, required guarantee type, and whether one representation can serve both phases.

Observable preservation: original indices, arrival order, mutation permission, grouping order, and duplicate semantics constrain legal transformations.
Lifecycle and resources: build, queries, updates, output, memory, mutation, and guarantee type determine which legal candidate is feasible and cheaper.

blocks.text: Immutability is a correctness constraint

Scan the array from left to right. For each value, first test whether it is already in a set; if so, a duplicate exists, otherwise insert it. The scan reads the original sequence but never writes or reorders it, so the byte-for-byte input contract is preserved.
After any prefix, the set contains at most one entry for each of the k distinct values seen so far. Its peak auxiliary state is therefore O(k), which becomes O(n) when all n values are distinct.

Comparing only original neighbors is legal but incomplete because equal values can begin far apart. blocks.text: Reuse input storage when mutation is legal

Sorting the original array groups equal values into adjacent positions. A single linear scan can then detect whether any neighboring pair is equal. Because the prompt permits reordering, the array itself can hold the sorted state instead of allocating one hash entry per distinct value.

An in-place heapsort can use O(1) auxiliary space; an in-place introsort commonly uses O(log n) stack. Either is asymptotically below an O(n) set while keeping the required O(n log n) worst-case bound, but the implementation-specific memory claim must be named.

blocks.text: A copied sort spends O(n) memory and loses the stated advantage. A set also reaches O(n) entries when all values are distinct. All-pairs comparison uses O(1) space but O(n²) time, so the new time bound excludes it. Reusable rule: a time-space tradeoff is meaningful only after both limits are in the prompt.

blocks.text: Sorting has no universal space bound

"Sorting" names a family of algorithms, not one implementation. Auxiliary space counts memory created during execution: a recursion stack, temporary merge buffer, decorated records, and any copy required because the original input may not change.

In-place heapsort can use O(1) auxiliary space, typical introsort uses O(log n) stack, and array merge sort commonly uses O(n) temporary storage. If the input is immutable, even the first two need an O(n) copy unless they sort a separate existing representation.
blocks.title: Three different profiles

blocks.text: Stability can further restrict the eligible implementations, but it does not by itself establish one universal bound. Reusable rule: never quote the space of an operation family; name the concrete algorithm, mutation policy, stability requirement, and live representations.

blocks.text: Count the state that remains live

A frequency table maps each distinct value to one counter. Repeated occurrences update an existing counter rather than allocate another logical entry, so after scanning n values the table contains k key-counter pairs.

Each of the k entries uses constant-size logical metadata under the question's model, giving O(k) auxiliary space. Since 1 ≤ k ≤ n for a nonempty input, heavy duplication can make k much smaller than n, while an all-distinct input makes k = n and yields O(n).

The sorting path's peak auxiliary space is the O(n) copy plus the chosen sort's stack or buffer. The comparison is therefore hash state versus copy-plus-sort state, not hash state versus a hypothetical free in-place sort.

An alias is another reference to the same array object. In-place sorting writes that shared object repeatedly; without a synchronization contract, a concurrent reader can observe a partially reordered sequence or race with those writes before the function has any chance to restore the final order.

Even if a routine tries to undo the sort, a callback or reader can observe intermediate state, and an exception can skip restoration. Copying before sorting isolates the writes at O(n) auxiliary cost; a hash scan can also leave the input untouched.

blocks.text: One query cannot amortize a reusable build

A missing target makes the direct scan inspect n values, so scan time is O(n). Building a set performs n expected O(1) insertions and one expected O(1) lookup, giving O(n + 1)=O(n) expected hash time.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and one binary search adds O(log n), so sort time is O(n log n + log n)=O(n log n). blocks.text: Why the moving window is legal

Maintain the sum of the inclusive window [left, right]. Advancing right adds a positive value, so an insufficient sum can only move toward the threshold. Once the sum reaches target, record the current length before removing a[left]; that removal produces the next shorter candidate ending at the same right. Repeat while the sum remains valid. When a removal makes the sum too small, further removals would only decrease it again, so no still-shorter window at this right can qualify and right must advance. This is the discard proof, not merely a loop template.

For a sum threshold, a simple variable window is justified only when extending right cannot lower the sum and removing left cannot raise it. With nonnegative values this lets the algorithm repair a boundary and discard candidates without needing to revisit them; an arbitrary negative value removes that proof.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Let m = r - l + 1. Starting a running sum at zero and visiting a[l], ..., a[r] reads exactly m values, so the query costs O(m) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Building P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] would first read all n values and retain n + 1 cumulative sums; it would then answer this one query as P[r + 1] - P[l]. O(n log n) may be an acceptable cost, and examples may increase confidence or reveal bugs, but neither explains why the algorithm cannot make an irreversible mistake on an untested instance. A greedy proof must connect the chosen local preference to a global optimum, such as by exchange, dominance, a stays-ahead invariant, or induction after a safe first choice.

More non-exhaustive examples never create that quantification. Sorting is compatible with many greedy methods and is not the defect. The review habit is to separate claims: implementation complexity, empirical behavior, feasibility, and optimality each require their own evidence. Tests are powerful for finding counterexamples; they are not a substitute for the correctness contract.

messages.text: Sort-then-greedy is a standard strategy shape. Greedy refers to the commitment rule, not the absence of preprocessing.
Unless the legal domain is exhaustively finite and fully enumerated, additional examples still do not prove the universal claim.

constraints: Projects can conflict with several other projects.

blocks.text:
A sort key must order candidates by a property that controls the residual problem or objective. Descending reward compares each project in isolation. If the first project conflicts with several others, its true consequence includes the value of every combination it removes. The note never proves that replacing those projects with the highest-reward project is no worse.

Descending order is not inherently invalid, and reward can be a legitimate numeric field in problems with the right exchange structure. The defect is the missing structural link, not the data type or direction. The transfer rule is to challenge words such as “obvious,” “natural,” or “largest” by asking what residual boundary the key improves and what optimal exchange it permits.

constraints: The document has not established a greedy-choice property.

blocks.text:
Dynamic programming can exploit optimal substructure while retaining several states that encode different histories or resource levels. Greedy commits to one local choice and removes competing possibilities. That stronger discard requires a greedy-choice property, exchange argument, dominance relation, or stays-ahead invariant. Without it, the fact that an optimal solution contains optimal subsolutions does not identify which first choice is safe.

Running time cannot make two incorrect and correct methods interchangeable, and both methods can solve optimization problems. Recursion is an implementation or proof form, not a strategy classification. The transfer rule is to ask what alternatives remain alive after each step. If multiple materially different states must be compared, dynamic programming may fit; if one state dominates all others by proof, greedy may fit.

messages.text: Optimization is a primary use of dynamic programming. This option reverses the method’s purpose.
Efficiency cannot supply a missing correctness property. A faster wrong algorithm is not interchangeable with a correct state-based one.
A recursive decomposition can still compare multiple choices. Greedy correctness depends on safe commitment, not on whether recursion is present.

feedback.reason: The methods share neither state retention nor proof obligations. Optimal substructure supports decomposition, but greedy additionally needs a theorem that discarding alternatives is safe.

options.text: Greedy is interchangeable with dynamic programming whenever it has lower running time.

blocks.text:
Total cost decomposes into immediate cost plus the best achievable residual cost. Minimizing only the first term is safe when the chosen action leaves a residual state no worse than the states produced by alternatives, or when an exchange proves that any optimum can use the choice. The explanation provides neither relation. It therefore assumes the exact local-to-global property that needs proof.

Complexity is a separate question, and renaming a quantity cannot change what it measures. The transfer test is to write the objective after the choice: localContribution(choice) + optimalResidual(choice). If the residual term varies and is not dominated by the greedy choice, the immediate comparison is incomplete. A valid greedy proof must control both terms.

messages.text: Greedy is a strategy family, not a definition that makes every local optimum global. The implication is the theorem to prove.
An efficient implementation can still return a suboptimal sequence. Correctness must be established before cost analysis closes the argument.

feedback.reason: The conclusion needs a bridge from the current metric to every future consequence. Without residual dominance, a cheap action now can force expensive actions later.

constraints: The objective is maximum selected count.

blocks.text:
Maximum-cardinality interval selection is governed by the end of the selected interval because that end determines which future intervals remain feasible. Earliest start can select a long interval that blocks several later intervals. Even if examples happen to avoid that case, they do not show that every optimum can be transformed to begin with the earliest-start choice. Finally, “non-overlapping” is incomplete until touching endpoints are classified, because the scan must choose between >= and > at the boundary.

Sorting itself is compatible with a correct earliest-finish greedy algorithm, and interval problems include both greedy-solvable and non-greedy variants. The review transfer template is: verify the local key controls the decisive residual state, require universal safety evidence, and surface all assumptions that alter feasibility before the learner answers.

blocks.text:
A feasibility invariant answers whether the current partial solution violates constraints. It does not compare that solution with alternatives that could have produced more value. To establish optimality, the proof needs a bridge such as an exchange that preserves value, a dominance relation, or an upper bound showing that no rejected alternative can improve the result.

Recursion is optional: some greedy proofs use induction, but induction still needs a safety statement for the next commitment. The transfer test is to separate the proof obligations explicitly: first ask whether every produced state is legal, then ask why the discarded feasible choices cannot lead to a better objective. Passing the first test never settles the second.

messages.text: Many feasible solutions can have different values. Feasibility is necessary but not sufficient for an optimization claim.
A greedy proof may be iterative, exchange-based, or invariant-based. Its missing ingredient is safety, not a particular proof format.

feedback.reason: Legality and optimality are different claims. A valid but low-value set can be produced by a completely feasible greedy sequence.

options.text: The conclusion is valid because a feasible result is automatically optimal when every addition was legal.

constraints: A prefix is considered feasible only when its total duration is within the current deadline.

blocks.text:
Equal deadlines activate the same constraint boundary, but different durations can change which job is removed or retained when the prefix becomes infeasible. If the proof relies on a particular selected set, heap state, or stable ordering, the tie rule is part of the algorithm contract. The author may instead prove a stronger permutation-invariance statement showing that every tie order yields an equally good result and preserves the claimed invariant.

Randomness does not remove a correctness obligation, and a value-based tie-break is not automatically safe: it must follow from the stated objective. The transfer rule is to inspect every equality case in a local ordering. Ask which non-key fields can influence future state; if any can, either define the tie-break or prove that it is immaterial.

messages.text: Random choice can select a bad order and makes reproducibility harder; it is not a proof of permutation invariance.

blocks.text:
If intervals are half-open, an interval beginning exactly at the previous end is compatible and >= is correct. If endpoints are closed or touching is defined as overlap, the acceptance condition changes. Tests with distinct endpoints cannot distinguish these contracts, so they provide no evidence for the equality branch.

The reviewer should require one explicit endpoint model, examples that exercise equality, and an implementation condition that matches the model. Neither strict nor non-strict comparison is universally safer. The transfer rule applies to all boundary-driven greedy algorithms: include equality, empty input, and zero-width cases in both the specification and the proof obligations.

blocks.text:
The phrase “best for the prefix” could mean maximum count, maximum value, minimum occupied resource, lexicographically smallest boundary, or something else. Those claims have different proof obligations. The proof must state the invariant precisely and show how the accepted prefix summarizes all information the suffix needs. If two prefixes have the same visible boundary but different future value, the claimed compression is false and more state may be required.

Examples can help discover the right invariant, but they cannot define it by implication. Variable naming is secondary. The transfer rule is to write a sentence of the form “after processing this prefix, the maintained state has property P, and no alternative state with the same resource boundary has a better objective value.” If that sentence cannot be made exact, the greedy argument is not ready.

messages.text: Examples may expose ambiguity but do not turn an undefined claim into a universal invariant.

constraints: The original equal-reward proof uses only the number of selected jobs.

blocks.text:
Greedy proofs are tied to the objective as well as to feasibility. In the equal-reward setting, replacing one selected job with another can be enough because both contribute one unit. With unequal rewards, the replacement may discard a high-value job or make a lower-value combination look equivalent when it is not. The same capacity argument may still support a different rule, but it cannot be reused without checking the value term.

Changing the heap does not repair a proof whose exchange statement has changed. The transfer rule is to compare the exact quantity preserved by each local replacement with the new objective. If the proof preserves cardinality while the problem optimizes weighted value, the proof is aimed at the wrong theorem.

blocks.text:
The endpoint model is part of the algorithm, not a formatting detail. A selected interval [a,currentEnd) occupies times t with a <= t < currentEnd. At t = currentEnd the resource is free, so [currentEnd,b) is compatible. Requiring a strict greater-than would incorrectly reject legal back-to-back intervals and could reduce the maximum count.

Checking candidate.end against currentEnd does not establish non-overlap because an interval can end later while starting inside the occupied range. The transfer rule is to derive the inequality from the domain contract. Closed intervals, discrete inclusive ranges, cleanup gaps, or travel time between meetings can require start > currentEnd or start >= currentEnd + gap. Hidden endpoint assumptions must not appear only in feedback.

constraints: Candidates are compared only if they are feasible against currentEnd=5.

blocks.text:
The scan performs two logically separate operations. First it filters candidates by compatibility: X starts at 4 and overlaps the selected interval, while Y starts exactly at 5 and is legal under half-open semantics; Z is also legal. Second it applies the greedy comparison among feasible candidates. Y ends at 7, earlier than Z at 9, so selecting Y leaves at least as much room for later intervals.

Choosing Z would still be feasible but would abandon the earliest-finish dominance that supports maximum cardinality. Selecting none would misuse endpoint semantics. This boundary application transfers to meetings, machine reservations, or event selection when the resource is reusable immediately and every accepted interval has equal value. Setup gaps or weights change the filter or objective.

questions.prompt: The last selected half-open interval ends at 5. Remaining candidates are X=[4,6), Y=[5,7), and Z=[7,9). Which interval should the canonical maximum-cardinality greedy scan select next?

constraints: There are n intervals.

blocks.text:
Any feasible non-overlapping remainder contains k intervals and removes n-k. Therefore minimizing removals is equivalent to maximizing k. The canonical earliest-finish scan computes a maximum-cardinality compatible subset, and subtraction gives the minimum number removed. No separate local removal heuristic is needed.

The equivalence relies on every interval contributing the same one-unit keep value and every removal having equal cost. If removals have different penalties, maximizing the count can discard an expensive interval and produce a poor cost. The transfer habit is to check whether two objectives are algebraic complements under identical item weights. When they are, the existing greedy proof transfers; when weights enter, the boundary changes.

feedback.reason: With equal keep value and equal removal cost, minimizing removals is exactly the complement of maximizing the compatible set. The same earliest-finish boundary applies.

questions.prompt: A problem asks for the minimum number of intervals to remove so the remaining intervals do not overlap. Every removal has equal cost. Which strategy-level reformulation is valid?

constraints: Weights are independent of start and end times.

blocks.text:
Earliest finish optimizes future capacity, not current weight. In the unweighted problem, exchanging one interval for another preserves the one-unit contribution. With arbitrary weights, the earlier-finishing interval may be worth far less, and the extra future room may not compensate. Conversely, choosing the heaviest interval can block a combination with greater total weight.

The usual diagnostic is to retain alternatives at a boundary such as the next compatible interval and compare include versus exclude value. That suggests dynamic programming, but this item stops at the strategy boundary rather than defining the recurrence. Greedy and dynamic programming are not interchangeable: greedy needs a local dominance theorem; dynamic programming can compare state-dependent continuations when that theorem is absent.

messages.text: Future room is only one part of the weighted objective. A feasible exchange can lose more weight than the extra room can recover.

blocks.text:
The earliest-finish selection algorithm answers “How many meetings can one room host if conflicts may be rejected?” Minimum rooms asks “How many resources are needed so every meeting is retained?” These outputs treat overlap in opposite ways. Selection removes conflicting intervals; room counting must preserve them and track how many are active at once.

A sweep of starts and ends or a min-heap of active end times can compute the peak. Endpoint tie rules still matter because a meeting ending at time t can release a room for one starting at t under half-open semantics. The transfer boundary is the output contract. Identical interval data can require different greedy invariants when the learner changes from selecting a subset to allocating resources.

feedback.reason: Room counting is a different archetype: overlaps are demand to accommodate, not conflicts to discard. The decisive quantity is peak concurrency, not the size of one compatible subset.

constraints: An interval is eligible for the next step only if start <= x.

blocks.text:
At point x, any next interval must begin at or before x or a gap appears. Among those eligible intervals, choosing the one with the farthest end dominates shorter-reaching choices for the current step: it uses one interval and leaves a residual uncovered suffix no larger than any alternative. If the greatest eligible end is at most x, no candidate crosses the current boundary and complete coverage is impossible. Otherwise update x to the chosen end and repeat until x >= T.

This is an interval greedy algorithm, but its key is the opposite of maximum compatible selection. In selection, an early end leaves room for more separate intervals. In coverage, a far end covers more of the required continuum with the same one-interval cost. The transfer lesson is to derive both the progress key and the failure condition from the output contract rather than memorizing “intervals imply earliest finish.”

messages.text: An early end makes less coverage progress and can force extra intervals. It is safe for a different objective: selecting many non-overlapping intervals.
Starting near x is irrelevant if the interval barely extends the covered prefix. Eligibility and reach are separate properties.
Short duration does not maximize how far the covered prefix advances; repeatedly taking short intervals can require extra intervals even when a farther-reaching eligible interval exists.

feedback.reason: Coverage minimizes the number of extensions, so the decisive boundary is how far the next eligible interval advances the covered prefix. Earliest finish optimizes a different interval objective.

blocks.text:
Greedy reasoning is about committing now without later reconsideration. The first accepted statement identifies the greedy-choice property: the preferred choice must be compatible with at least one global optimum, commonly shown by exchange, dominance, or a stays-ahead argument. The second identifies the recursive structure needed after that commitment: once the choice is fixed, the rest of the instance must still express the same objective with a smaller feasible region.

Neither condition is established by syntax. Almost any finite record set can be sorted, and many incorrect heuristics can be written as one pass. Sorting by amount replaces the order used by the first rule and does not make equal customer IDs contiguous. Even a perfectly implemented adjacent scan would therefore solve a different problem. The first defect is the unjustified preprocessing assumption, not loop length or numeric comparability.

For (time, customer, amount) events (1, A, 100), (2, B, 1), (3, A, 2), (4, B, 3), customer A is first to repeat and its earliest event is at time 1. Amount sorting produces B, A, B, A: neither customer's equal IDs are adjacent, and the order no longer identifies which second occurrence happened first.

blocks.text: Each review step depends on facts established by the preceding one, so changing the order risks proving properties of the wrong problem.

items: State the external contract first: required order, source identities, mutation rights, and resource limits define what counts as a legal result.
Inspect the sort relation next: its key and tie rules must expose the exact adjacency, grouping, or monotonicity used downstream.
Verify the consumer under that established order: prove that its scan, runs, or pointer moves cannot discard a valid candidate.
Finally recompute time, extra space, and side effects for the complete implementation; these properties cannot rescue an algorithm that is already semantically wrong.

blocks.text: Candidate generation and final selection serve different purposes. A complete enumeration explicitly checks every legal pair, so it clarifies the answer contract and can act as a trusted reference: on small inputs, compare an optimized candidate's output with the enumeration's output to expose correctness bugs. Its repeated computations or searches also reveal work that a faster approach might replace with an index, ordering, or amortized state. The later feasibility gate rejects O(n²) work at the target maximum while retaining this explanatory and testing role. The transfer rule is to distinguish a reference candidate used to establish correctness from a deployable candidate required to meet the operation budget.

blocks.text: A reusable strategy is justified only when all four gates hold:

Amortization: setup + maintenance + q·indexedQueryCost is no worse than the relevant alternative for the actual workload.
Validity: updates either do not occur or can maintain the index within the operation budget, so answers never use stale state.
Resource fit: construction latency and retained memory stay within their hard limits.

Repeated use is a signal to calculate amortization, not proof of a win. The statement becomes true only after the saved work exceeds setup and maintenance under the resource limits.
Without a break-even check, setup may cost more than the work it saves over the actual number of queries.
Without a compatibility check, preprocessing may optimize a related operation while failing some legal query shapes or semantics.

questions.prompt: Daily advertising costs are nonnegative and B ≥ 0. A campaign planner wants the longest consecutive run whose total cost is at most B. Which strategy-selection rule transfers, and what boundary must be remembered?

constraints: Badge IDs arrive one at a time.
The answer is required immediately.
The question is exact, not approximate.

blocks.text: Badge IDs are merely keys. The decisive signals are incremental arrival, an answer due before future data is known, and exact membership in the current event history. For each arriving ID x:

items: Check whether x is in the seen-ID set.
If it is present, emit the duplicate alert immediately.
Insert x so later arrivals can detect it.

blocks.text: Checking before insertion distinguishes a prior occurrence from the current badge itself. End-of-event sorting could answer an offline audit but misses immediate alerts, and pointer placement has no ordered discard rule. A bounded recent-history contract would require state eviction, while approximate membership would require an explicitly relaxed correctness contract.

messages.text: This is a legal offline audit candidate but violates the immediate-answer timing. It becomes appropriate when alerts may be delayed until the full event log is available.
A sequence alone does not supply the ordering invariant needed for pointer elimination. Two pointers become useful only after an ordered relation or window contract is established.

feedback.reason: The underlying contract is online exact membership over a growing prefix. Retained seen-state supports the required answer time.

options.text: Wait until the event ends, sort all IDs, and then report duplicates.
Keep pointers at the first and latest badge because two pointers work on sequences.
Maintain a set of previously seen IDs and test membership before insertion.

questions.prompt: A venue receives badge IDs one at a time and must immediately flag an ID that has appeared earlier in the same event. Which strategy-selection rule transfers?

constraints: Daily values are immutable.
Queries are numerous.
Each query asks for an additive date interval.

blocks.text: The surface form uses days and cash flow, but the decision contract is an immutable sequence with many additive range queries. Define P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + flow[i] once; the inclusive total from day l through r is P[r + 1] − P[l] because subtraction cancels every earlier day shared by both prefixes. Sorting would destroy calendar contiguity, while a set answers presence rather than an aggregate. Updates, non-additive queries, or output requiring individual transactions would change the mechanism. The general rule is to map the new story to structure, operation, and lifecycle before reusing a strategy.

messages.text: A date set can answer whether a day exists, but not the sum over a range. It becomes useful if the query primitive changes to exact membership.
Ordering by value breaks the date interval that defines each query. Sorting becomes relevant only for value-rank or threshold questions that do not depend on original chronology.

feedback.reason: The decisive structure is a static additive range query, independent of the finance vocabulary. Cumulative state supports repeated interval totals.

options.text: Store each date in a hash set and use exact date membership as the reusable operation for computing every requested interval total.
Treat days as a static sequence, build cumulative totals once, and recover each interval by subtracting two prefixes.
Sort the daily totals by value, then answer each requested date interval from the corresponding segment of the sorted sequence.

questions.prompt: A finance tool stores one immutable daily net-flow value for a year and must answer thousands of questions such as 'What was the total flow from day l through day r?' Which prior strategy decision transfers most directly?

blocks.text: For each ID, check membership before adding it. The set is the minimum retained history needed for arbitrary earlier duplicates. Sorting after collection cannot emit prefix answers, and limiting history to a window changes the duplicate definition.

messages.text: Binary search requires ordered state that is not present.
It delays answers and cannot satisfy the per-arrival output contract.
A duplicate may be separated by any number of intervening events.

feedback.reason: The online and no-replay contract transfers the membership-state strategy, not an offline preprocessing strategy.

options.text: Maintain a seen-ID set online, query it before insertion, then insert the current ID.
Sort the complete stream after it ends, which still answers every earlier prefix immediately.
Keep only the last two IDs because duplicate detection concerns adjacent events.
Binary-search the arrival order without maintaining sorted state.

questions.prompt: A log stream arrives once, cannot be replayed, and must report whether each event ID has appeared earlier. Which transferred mechanism fits?

constraints: Speed is an integer in a known bounded range.
Feasibility can be checked for a proposed speed.
Greater speed never reduces completed work.
At least one speed in the range is feasible.

blocks.text: The target is not an existing element but the smallest parameter satisfying a constraint. If increasing speed cannot make completion harder, feasibility is upward-closed: insufficient speeds form a prefix and sufficient speeds a suffix. That boundary licenses half discard, while the total cost is logarithmic in the speed range times the check cost. Sorting jobs may be part of the feasibility check but does not by itself search the speed domain. The transfer boundary is nonmonotonic behaviour, such as speeds that introduce failures or discrete modes where faster can become infeasible.

messages.text: A set records which speeds were tried but provides no rule for choosing informative trials or proving untried values impossible. It becomes relevant only as memoization inside another search.

Job ordering may help evaluate one candidate speed, but it does not locate the minimum parameter without a search or derivation. It becomes complete only if a proof directly computes the optimum after sorting.

feedback.reason: The unfamiliar surface still exposes an ordered answer domain and a monotonic feasibility predicate, which is the decision boundary for binary search on answer.

options.text: Sort jobs by duration; sorting alone always reveals the minimum speed.
Prove that any speed above a feasible speed is also feasible, then binary-search the first feasible speed.
Insert tried speeds into a set and choose the smallest stored value.

questions.prompt: A production line must choose the minimum integer machine speed that completes all jobs before a deadline. A deterministic check can decide whether a proposed speed is sufficient, and the known bounded speed range contains at least one feasible value. Which strategy-selection rule transfers?

constraints: Return the first taller building to the right.
Original street order must be preserved.
Each building needs at most one witness.

blocks.text: Street position supplies left-to-right processing order, while height supplies the strict comparison:

items: For the current building j, pop every top index i whose height is strictly smaller and record j as i's first taller witness.
Do not pop an equal height: equal is not taller, so that index remains unresolved.
Push j. The stack heights are non-increasing, and every retained index has seen no taller building so far.

blocks.text: When an index is popped, the current building is its first valid witness because every intermediate building has already been processed. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving amortized O(n) work. Sorting loses 'first to the right,' while an ordinary unpruned stack lacks the resolution rule. Asking for every taller building would increase output and invalidate permanent discard.

messages.text: Retaining history without a monotonic invariant provides no efficient resolution rule. It becomes useful only if another mechanism searches that history or if LIFO order is itself the output contract.
Height order does not preserve street order or nearest-right identity. Sorting becomes relevant for global rank questions rather than directional nearest witnesses.

feedback.reason: The task is a next-greater relation. A monotonic stack keeps exactly the unresolved frontier and discards entries when their first valid witness appears.

options.text: Sort buildings by height, then use adjacent taller values to determine the first greater building for every original street position.
Maintain a non-increasing stack of unresolved building indices; a taller building resolves and pops strictly shorter indices.
Push every building onto an ordinary stack and never remove anything until the end.

questions.prompt: For each building in a street, return the first building to its right that is taller. Which prior mechanism transfers despite the new surface?

constraints: Values change after nearly every query.
Queries ask for medians, not sums.
The question tests transfer boundary, not replacement implementation.

blocks.text: The original scalar prefix-sum rule relied on two facts: the data snapshot stayed stable, and an additive total could be isolated by subtracting cumulative totals. Here almost every update makes that static array stale, and subtracting two scalar sums cannot recover the value ordering needed for a median. A richer update-aware order-statistics representation may exist, but many queries cannot make this insufficient state correct. The transfer rule is to re-check output, update model, state sufficiency, and invariant even when the new prompt uses familiar nouns.

messages.text: Query volume justifies evaluating preprocessing, but cannot make an incompatible representation correct. It becomes relevant after a legal update-aware median mechanism is identified.
Range describes the selected positions, not the aggregate or update lifecycle. The claim becomes true only when the new operation and stability assumptions match the original invariant.

feedback.reason: Transfer follows preserved mechanism and preconditions, not shared vocabulary. Frequent updates and median queries remove the static additive cancellation that prefix sums require.

options.text: Reuse prefix sums because the large query count makes preprocessing valuable, even if updates and median output change what the stored state must support.
Reuse prefix sums unchanged because the selected positions are still ranges, so the familiar range-query label is enough to preserve the original strategy.
Both the update lifecycle and the non-cancellable median aggregate differ, so the stored prefix-sum invariant cannot answer the new contract.

questions.prompt: A dashboard asks many range questions, but values are updated after nearly every query and each query asks for the median of the current range. Why does a static prefix-sum decision not transfer merely from the word range?

blocks.text: A prefix sum answers static ranges cheaply but becomes stale after an update. A dynamic index may support logarithmic updates and queries, subject to memory and constants. Contiguity alone does not turn arbitrary online ranges into one moving window.

messages.text: Answers would use stale data unless the prefix structure is rebuilt or maintained.
Sorting values does not maintain positional range sums.
Queries can arrive in arbitrary order and refer to arbitrary ranges.

feedback.reason: The new update model changes index lifetime and maintenance cost even though the query surface still says range.

options.text: A static prefix-sum strategy no longer remains valid without rebuilds; compare a maintained dynamic range structure against update/query volume.
Keep the prefix array because the query wording is unchanged.
Use a moving window because every range query is contiguous.
Sort after every update because sorting always maintains sums.

questions.prompt: A new domain asks thousands of range totals on immutable values, then changes the values to support frequent point updates. Which transfer boundary matters?

blocks.text: If the smallest plus largest is below C, the smallest cannot pair with any remaining value to reach C; if above, the largest cannot. The candidate is an arbitrary pair, not a contiguous range, so window and prefix-sum rules do not transfer.

messages.text: Choosing one endpoint without the complementary elimination comparison is not a complete proof.
A pair sum is not an interval sum, even when indices have a numeric order.
The output selects two values, not every value in an interval.

feedback.reason: Sortedness makes an endpoint comparison eliminate all pairs involving one endpoint in the relevant direction.

options.text: Use two endpoints; if their sum is too small advance the lower value, and if too large retreat the higher value under sorted-order elimination.
Shrink a contiguous range while its total exceeds C; pair output is a window contract.
Build prefix sums because two distinct positions always form a range.
Always choose the smallest package because it leaves the most capacity.

questions.prompt: A new problem supplies already sorted package weights and asks whether two distinct packages sum to capacity C. Which proof transfers directly?

constraints: Weights are already sorted.
Two distinct shipments are required.
Only existence is requested.

blocks.text: The logistics vocabulary changes none of the structural facts: there is an ordered sequence, a two-element sum target, and an existence output. The lightest remaining item cannot reach the target with any smaller partner when the current maximum partner is still too small; the symmetric argument removes the heaviest when the sum is too large. Hashing and repeated binary search can be legal alternatives, but the existing order makes a single O(n) pointer pass with O(1) extra state especially direct. If one witness pair were required, the same pointers could return their current indices because the input is already sorted. The transfer boundary is lost ordering, enumeration of all matching pairs, or a relation whose comparison does not eliminate an endpoint.

messages.text: Repeated binary search is legal on sorted data but costs O(n log n) and duplicates searches. It becomes relevant when pointer monotonicity is unavailable or the query structure differs.
Hashing is a candidate, not a universal requirement. It becomes preferable when the input is unsorted, expected-time lookup is acceptable, and extra memory fits.

feedback.reason: Sorted order makes the sum comparison a safe endpoint-elimination rule, so the pair-sum invariant transfers directly.

options.text: For every shipment, binary-search its complement in the remaining sorted weights; this is the only strategy that should exploit the order.
Build a hash set because pair-sum tasks require complement lookup, even when the weights are already sorted and can support ordered elimination.
Use opposite-end pointers; a sum below C eliminates the current lightest shipment, and a sum above C eliminates the current heaviest.

questions.prompt: Shipment weights are already sorted. The system must determine whether two distinct shipments exactly fill capacity C. Which prior strategy-selection rule transfers most directly?
